nodes.name: Run transformation
nodes.notes: Start here: click 'Execute workflow' to build and publish the analytics tables once. Run the cleaning stage first, so clean.* is filled. In Week 3 the orchestrator calls this instead.

nodes.name: Every night
nodes.notes: Schedule Trigger, 02:00 every night, switched off (disabled). In Week 3 the orchestrator runs the whole pipeline on a schedule instead; to run only this stage at night, enable this node and publish the workflow.

parameters.jsCode:
// ==== Settings ===============================================================
const ONLY = [];          // e.g. ['kpi_summary'] to build a few views; empty = all
const FRESH_SQL = false;  // true = ask the agent for new SQL even when a view already has SQL that passed
// =============================================================================

const runId = 'transform_' + new Date().toISOString().replace(/[-:T]/g, '').slice(0, 14);

// Business definitions. The agent gets them with every question; the reference SQL below follows them exactly.
const DEFINITIONS = [
  "A counted order is a row in clean.orders whose order_status is not null and not 'canceled' or 'unavailable', " +
    'and that has at least one row in clean.order_items. Every view counts only these orders.',
  'Revenue = sum(coalesce(price, 0) + coalesce(freight_value, 0)) over the clean.order_items rows of counted orders.',
  'orders = the number of distinct counted orders. customers = the number of distinct customer_unique_id ' +
    '(from clean.customers) of counted orders.',
  'avg_order_value = revenue / orders.',
  'Round money and averages to 2 decimals with round(x, 2), once, on the final value.',
];

const RELATIONSHIPS = [
  'clean.order_items.order_id → clean.orders.order_id (an order has one or more items)',
  'clean.orders.customer_id → clean.customers.customer_id (customer_unique_id identifies the person across orders)',
  'clean.order_items.product_id → clean.products.product_id',
  'clean.order_items.seller_id → clean.sellers.seller_id',
  'clean.products.product_category_name → clean.category_translation.product_category_name ' +
    '(English name in product_category_name_english)',
  'clean.payments.order_id → clean.orders.order_id (an order can have several payments)',
  'clean.reviews.order_id → clean.orders.order_id (an order can have more than one review)',
  'Some IDs may have no match in the linked table after cleaning.',
];

// Building blocks of the reference SQL (the answer key). The agent never sees these.
const COUNTED = `select o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.order_purchase_timestamp from clean.orders o
  where o.order_status is not null and o.order_status not in ('canceled', 'unavailable')
    and exists (select 1 from clean.order_items i where i.order_id = o.order_id)`;
const ITEMS = `select i.order_id, i.product_id, coalesce(i.price, 0) + coalesce(i.freight_value, 0) as revenue
  from clean.order_items i join (${COUNTED}) c on c.order_id = i.order_id`;
const WITH = `with c as (${COUNTED}), r as (${ITEMS})`;
const REVENUE = (where = '') => `${WITH} select sum(r.revenue) from r join c on c.order_id = r.order_id ${where}`;

// One entry per view. columns: name → [type, meaning]. grain: the columns that make a row unique (none = one row).
// indexes: built on the published analytics table, for the filters the dashboard uses.
const questions = [
  { view: 'orders_wide',
    question: 'One row per counted order with everything the dashboard filters and groups orders by: customer, ' +
              'state, dates, delivery time, lateness, items, revenue, payment and review.',
    columns: {
      order_id: ['text', 'the order'],
      customer_unique_id: ['text', 'the customer (null when the customer is unknown)'],
      customer_city: ['text', "the customer's city"],
      customer_state: ['text', "the customer's state"],
      order_status: ['text', 'order_status'],
      purchase_timestamp: ['timestamp', 'order_purchase_timestamp'],
      purchase_month: ['date', "date_trunc('month', order_purchase_timestamp)::date"],
      delivered_timestamp: ['timestamp', 'order_delivered_customer_date'],
      estimated_delivery_date: ['timestamp', 'order_estimated_delivery_date'],
      delivery_days: ['integer', 'order_delivered_customer_date::date - order_purchase_timestamp::date (null when not delivered)'],
      is_late: ['boolean', 'order_delivered_customer_date::date > order_estimated_delivery_date::date (null when either is missing)'],
      items: ['integer', 'number of order_items rows'],
      revenue: ['numeric', 'revenue of the order'],
      payment_value: ['numeric', 'sum of payment_value in clean.payments (null when there is no payment)'],
      main_payment_type: ['text', 'payment_type of the largest payment; on a tie, the lowest payment_sequential (null when there is no payment)'],
      review_score: ['numeric', 'average review_score of the reviews of the order (null when there is none)'] },
    grain: ['order_id'],
    notes: 'Keep orders whose customer is missing from clean.customers (customer columns null). Aggregate payments ' +
           'and reviews per order before joining, so an order never repeats.',
    indexes: [['purchase_month'], ['customer_state'], ['order_status']],
    reference_sql: `${WITH},
      items as (select order_id, count(*)::int as items, sum(revenue) as revenue from r group by order_id),
      pay as (select order_id, sum(payment_value) as payment_value from clean.payments group by order_id),
      main_pay as (select distinct on (order_id) order_id, payment_type from clean.payments
                   order by order_id, payment_value desc nulls last, payment_sequential),
      rev as (select order_id, round(avg(review_score), 2) as review_score from clean.reviews group by order_id)
      select o.order_id, cu.customer_unique_id, cu.customer_city, cu.customer_state, o.order_status,
             o.order_purchase_timestamp as purchase_timestamp,
             date_trunc('month', o.order_purchase_timestamp)::date as purchase_month,
             o.order_delivered_customer_date as delivered_timestamp,
             o.order_estimated_delivery_date as estimated_delivery_date,
             o.order_delivered_customer_date::date - o.order_purchase_timestamp::date as delivery_days,
             o.order_delivered_customer_date::date > o.order_estimated_delivery_date::date as is_late,
             it.items, round(it.revenue, 2) as revenue, round(p.payment_value, 2) as payment_value,
             mp.payment_type as main_payment_type, rv.review_score
      from c join clean.orders o on o.order_id = c.order_id
           join items it on it.order_id = o.order_id
           left join clean.customers cu on cu.customer_id = o.customer_id
           left join pay p on p.order_id = o.order_id
           left join main_pay mp on mp.order_id = o.order_id
           left join rev rv on rv.order_id = o.order_id`,
    reconcile: { column: 'revenue', expected_sql: REVENUE() } },

  { view: 'order_items_wide',
    question: 'One row per item of a counted order with everything the dashboard filters items by: month, state, ' +
              'product, category, seller and revenue.',
    columns: {
      order_id: ['text', 'the order'],
      order_item_id: ['integer', 'the item number within the order'],
      purchase_month: ['date', "date_trunc('month', order_purchase_timestamp)::date"],
      customer_state: ['text', "the customer's state (null when the customer is unknown)"],
      product_id: ['text', 'the product'],
      category: ['text', "English category name; the Portuguese name when there is no translation; 'unknown' when the product or its category is missing"],
      seller_id: ['text', 'the seller'],
      seller_state: ['text', "the seller's state (null when the seller is unknown)"],
      price: ['numeric', 'price'],
      freight_value: ['numeric', 'freight_value'],
      revenue: ['numeric', 'coalesce(price, 0) + coalesce(freight_value, 0)'] },
    grain: ['order_id', 'order_item_id'],
    notes: 'Keep every item of a counted order: use left joins for customers, products, categories and sellers.',
    indexes: [['purchase_month'], ['customer_state'], ['category'], ['seller_id'], ['order_id']],
    reference_sql: `${WITH}
      select i.order_id, i.order_item_id, date_trunc('month', c.order_purchase_timestamp)::date as purchase_month,
             cu.customer_state, i.product_id,
             coalesce(t.product_category_name_english, p.product_category_name, 'unknown') as category,
             i.seller_id, s.seller_state, i.price, i.freight_value,
             round(coalesce(i.price, 0) + coalesce(i.freight_value, 0), 2) as revenue
      from clean.order_items i join c on c.order_id = i.order_id
           left join clean.customers cu on cu.customer_id = c.customer_id
           left join clean.products p on p.product_id = i.product_id
           left join clean.category_translation t on t.product_category_name = p.product_category_name
           left join clean.sellers s on s.seller_id = i.seller_id`,
    reconcile: { column: 'revenue', expected_sql: REVENUE() } },

  { view: 'kpi_summary',
    question: 'What are the headline numbers: total revenue, orders, customers, average order value and average review score?',
    columns: {
      revenue: ['numeric', 'total revenue'],
      orders: ['integer', 'number of counted orders'],
      customers: ['integer', 'number of distinct customers (customer_unique_id)'],
      avg_order_value: ['numeric', 'revenue / orders'],
      avg_review_score: ['numeric', 'average review_score of the reviews of counted orders (ignore null scores)'] },
    grain: [],
    reference_sql: `${WITH}
      select round((select sum(revenue) from r), 2) as revenue,
             (select count(*) from c)::int as orders,
             (select count(distinct cu.customer_unique_id) from c join clean.customers cu on cu.customer_id = c.customer_id)::int as customers,
             round((select sum(revenue) from r) / nullif((select count(*) from c), 0), 2) as avg_order_value,
             (select round(avg(rv.review_score), 2) from clean.reviews rv join c on c.order_id = rv.order_id) as avg_review_score`,
    reconcile: { column: 'revenue', expected_sql: REVENUE() } },

  { view: 'monthly_revenue',
    question: 'How do revenue and orders develop month by month (by purchase date)?',
    columns: {
      month: ['date', "first day of the purchase month: date_trunc('month', order_purchase_timestamp)::date"],
      orders: ['integer', 'counted orders purchased in that month'],
      revenue: ['numeric', 'revenue of those orders'],
      avg_order_value: ['numeric', 'revenue / orders for the month'] },
    grain: ['month'],
    indexes: [['month']],
    notes: 'Leave out orders without a purchase date.',
    reference_sql: `${WITH}
      select date_trunc('month', c.order_purchase_timestamp)::date as month,
             count(distinct c.order_id)::int as orders,
             round(sum(r.revenue), 2) as revenue,
             round(sum(r.revenue) / count(distinct c.order_id), 2) as avg_order_value
      from c join r on r.order_id = c.order_id
      where c.order_purchase_timestamp is not null
      group by 1`,
    reconcile: { column: 'revenue', expected_sql: REVENUE('where c.order_purchase_timestamp is not null') } },

  { view: 'revenue_by_state',
    question: 'How are revenue, orders and customers spread across the customer states?',
    columns: {
      customer_state: ['text', "the customer's state (null when the order's customer is unknown)"],
      orders: ['integer', 'counted orders from that state'],
      customers: ['integer', 'distinct customers (customer_unique_id) from that state'],
      revenue: ['numeric', 'revenue of those orders'] },
    grain: ['customer_state'],
    notes: 'Keep orders whose customer is missing from clean.customers, in a row with customer_state null.',
    reference_sql: `${WITH}
      select cu.customer_state,
             count(distinct c.order_id)::int as orders,
             count(distinct cu.customer_unique_id)::int as customers,
             round(sum(r.revenue), 2) as revenue
      from c join r on r.order_id = c.order_id
           left join clean.customers cu on cu.customer_id = c.customer_id
      group by cu.customer_state`,
    reconcile: { column: 'revenue', expected_sql: REVENUE() } },

  { view: 'top_categories',
    question: 'Which product categories bring in the most revenue?',
    columns: {
      category: ['text', "English category name; the Portuguese name when there is no translation; 'unknown' when the product or its category is missing"],
      items_sold: ['integer', 'order_items rows of counted orders in this category'],
      orders: ['integer', 'distinct counted orders with at least one item in this category'],
      revenue: ['numeric', 'revenue of those items'],
      revenue_rank: ['integer', 'rank() by revenue, highest first (1 = top category)'] },
    grain: ['category'],
    notes: 'Include every category, not only the top ones: the dashboard picks the top 10 with revenue_rank.',
    reference_sql: `${WITH}
      select coalesce(t.product_category_name_english, p.product_category_name, 'unknown') as category,
             count(*)::int as items_sold,
             count(distinct r.order_id)::int as orders,
             round(sum(r.revenue), 2) as revenue,
             rank() over (order by sum(r.revenue) desc)::int as revenue_rank
      from r left join clean.products p on p.product_id = r.product_id
             left join clean.category_translation t on t.product_category_name = p.product_category_name
      group by 1`,
    reconcile: { column: 'revenue', expected_sql: REVENUE() } },
];

// Stored SQL is used again only while the question, its columns and the definitions stay the same
const hash = s => [...s].reduce((h, ch) => (h * 33 + ch.charCodeAt(0)) >>> 0, 5381).toString(36);

return questions
  .filter(q => ONLY.length === 0 || ONLY.includes(q.view))
  .map(q => ({ json: {
    ...q, notes: q.notes ?? '', run_id: runId, fresh_sql: FRESH_SQL,
    definitions: DEFINITIONS, relationships: RELATIONSHIPS,
    spec_hash: hash(JSON.stringify([q.question, q.columns, q.grain, q.notes ?? '', DEFINITIONS])),
    // What transform.validate_view checks the view against
    spec: { columns: Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(q.columns).map(([c, [type]]) => [c, type])),
            grain: q.grain, min_rows: 1, reference_sql: q.reference_sql, reconcile: q.reconcile },
  } }));

nodes.name: Questions
nodes.notes: Settings and the question catalogue. ONLY limits the run to a few views; FRESH_SQL = true asks the agent for new SQL even when a view already has SQL that passed. Each question has the view name, the columns it must return, its key (grain) and a hand-written reference SQL: the answer key the agent's view must match, plus the indexes of its published table. The business definitions (which orders count, what revenue is) are shared by all questions. To add a view, add one entry.

nodes.name: Each question
nodes.notes: Loop Over Items, one question at a time. 'loop' output = build the next view; 'done' output (every view passed) = publish the tables.

parameters.query:
=-- The latest SQL for this view that passed validation (no row = never built)
select model_id, run_id, spec_hash, select_sql, explanation, assumptions
from ops.transform_models
where view_name = '{{ $('Each question').first().json.view }}' and status = 'passed'
order by created_at desc
limit 1;

nodes.name: Get stored SQL
nodes.notes: Looks up the latest SQL for this view that passed validation, in ops.transform_models. No row means the view was never built ('Always Output Data' is on).

parameters.query:
=-- The columns of every clean table, so the agent writes SQL against what is really there
select string_agg(format('clean.%s (%s)', table_name, cols), E'\n' order by table_name) as schema_text
from (select table_name, string_agg(column_name || ' ' || data_type, ', ' order by ordinal_position) as cols
      from information_schema.columns
      where table_schema = 'clean'
      group by table_name) t;

nodes.name: Get schema
nodes.notes: Reads the columns and types of every clean table from information_schema, so the agent sees the tables as they really are.

nodes.name: Build prompt
nodes.notes: Puts the question, the required columns, the business definitions, the clean schema and how the tables link into one prompt. No data rows and no reference SQL are sent. Also decides, without AI, whether the agent is needed: no stored SQL, the question changed, or FRESH_SQL.

nodes.name: SQL needed?
nodes.notes: true → ask the Transformation agent. false → use the stored SQL (still validated again).

options.systemMessage:
You are the transformation agent in a data pipeline. You answer one business question with one
PostgreSQL SELECT statement. The system saves it as a view in the models schema, then checks it: the columns, one
row per key, the revenue total against the source tables, and the numbers against a hand-written answer. If any check
fails, the view is not changed. Views that pass are published as tables for the dashboard.

Rules for the SQL:
- One SELECT (WITH ... SELECT is fine). No semicolon, no comments, nothing that writes or changes data.
- Read only from the clean schema, and always write the schema: clean.orders, not orders.
- Return exactly the columns asked for, with exactly those names, and no others.
- Follow the business definitions exactly. They decide which orders count and how revenue is computed.
- Joins can repeat rows (an order has several items, payments and reviews): use count(distinct ...) where needed, and
  never sum revenue over a join that repeats items.
- Join only along the links listed. Use left joins for lookups (customers, products, categories) so no revenue is lost.
- Cast counts to integer (::int). Round with round(x, 2) on the final value; cast to numeric first if x is not numeric.
- No ORDER BY or LIMIT: the dashboard sorts and picks.

explanation: two or three plain sentences for a business reader: which tables, which filters, how the numbers are
computed. assumptions: anything the question left open that you decided (may be empty).

nodes.name: Transformation agent
nodes.notes: AI agent (FR-T1). Writes one SELECT that answers the question, plus a plain explanation and its assumptions. It cannot run anything itself. Continues on error.

nodes.name: Transformation model
nodes.notes: The LLM the Transformation agent uses (Gemini 2.5 Flash, temperature 0). Needs the Gemini credential, like the other agents.

nodes.name: Transformation output format
nodes.notes: Structured Output Parser with a fixed JSON schema: select_sql, explanation, assumptions.

nodes.name: Use stored SQL
nodes.notes: Passes on the SQL that passed in an earlier run, in the same shape as the agent's answer. No AI call.

nodes.name: Check SQL
nodes.notes: Guardrails, deterministic, no AI: one statement, starting with SELECT or WITH, no comments, no writing keywords, only the clean schema, no system functions. Builds the script that creates the view as role transform_agent and validates it. A failed guardrail becomes an error in the next node, so nothing runs.

nodes.name: Create and validate view
nodes.notes: One transaction (FR-T2, FR-T3): switch to role transform_agent (can only read clean.* and create views in models), replace models.<view>, switch back and run transform.validate_view: columns, row count, no duplicate keys, revenue equals the clean tables, numbers match the reference SQL. Any failure rolls the transaction back, so the previous view stays. Continues on error.

nodes.name: Read result
nodes.notes: Reads the checks (or the error) and prepares an ops.transform_models row and an ops.agent_logs row with the SQL, the explanation and every check (FR-T5).

nodes.notes: Writes both rows.

nodes.name: Passed?
nodes.notes: true → next question. false → give the agent one try to fix its SQL.

nodes.notes: One transaction: copies each models.<view> into the table analytics.<view> (emptied and refilled, so Metabase's questions keep working), adds its indexes, grants the reader role and records the time in analytics.refresh_status. If anything fails, every table keeps the last good run.

parameters.content:
## Transformation stage · how it works

1. **Write SQL** (per question in *Questions*): the **Transformation agent** gets the question, the columns the view must return, the business definitions and the clean schema, and writes one SELECT. Views that passed before reuse their stored SQL (no AI call).
2. **Guardrails** (*Check SQL*, no AI): one read-only SELECT on `clean.*`, nothing else.
3. **Create + validate** in one transaction: the view is created in `models` as the restricted role `transform_agent`, then `transform.validate_view` checks columns, row count, duplicate keys, revenue against the clean tables and the numbers against a hand-written reference query. Any failure rolls back.
4. **One repair try**: the agent sees why its SQL failed and tries again. Fails twice → the run **stops** and nothing is published.
5. **Publish**: when every view passed, all of them are copied into **tables** in `analytics` in one transaction. Metabase reads only these, so the dashboard is ready whenever the pipeline last ran (e.g. at night).

Every SQL, with its checks, is in `ops.transform_models` and `ops.agent_logs`; `analytics.refresh_status` says when each table was published.
